findings.issue: Source says he “drew twelve youths alive out of the water”; candidate says he “dragged” them out, which sharpens the action (and the next sentence already says “pulled”).
findings.fix: At once the hero leaned his spear against a tamarisk bush and left it on the bank. Armed with his sword alone, he plunged into the river like a god. His purpose was grim, and he hewed the Trojans down on every side. They groaned horribly as they died under the sword, and the river ran red with blood. As fish flee in fear from a huge dolphin and fill every nook and corner of some fair harbor—for the dolphin is sure to eat all it can catch—so the Trojans cowered under the banks of the mighty river. When Achilles’s arms grew tired of killing, he drew twelve youths alive out of the water, to sacrifice in revenge for Patroclus son of Menoetius. He pulled them out like dazed fawns, tied their hands behind them with the belts of their own shirts, and handed them over to his men to take back to the ships. Then he sprang into the river again, thirsting for still more blood.

findings.issue: Source: “The dark waters of the river stood upright and would have overwhelmed the son of Peleus”. Candidate adds a simile not in the source (“stood up like a wall”) and turns the counterfactual into “was about to crash down”.
findings.fix: With that, the river raised his roaring flood high against Achilles. It seethed with foam, blood and the bodies of the dead. The dark waters of the river stood upright and would have overwhelmed the son of Peleus, but Hera was afraid that Achilles would be swept away in the great torrent, and she cried out loudly to her son Hephaestus. “Crook-foot,” she called, “my child, get up and act! I think it is you Xanthus wants to fight. Help us at once and light a fierce fire. Meanwhile I will bring the west wind and the white south wind up from the sea in a mighty hurricane. It will carry the flames against the heads and armor of the Trojans and burn them up. You, for your part, go along the banks of Xanthus, burning his trees and wrapping him in fire. Do not let him turn you back, whether he speaks kindly or harshly. Do not ease off until I shout to you. Then you may stop your flames.”

findings.issue: Source “took visible spear”; candidate resolves it to “took his spear” (Diomedes’s). Consistent with the poem but the source does not say whose spear.
Source “the corn lands of the plain”; candidate “the wheat fields of the plain” names a specific crop Butler does not.
findings.fix: As he spoke, his strong hand hurled the javelin, and the spear struck Achilles on the leg below the knee. The greave of newly worked tin rang loudly, but the spear bounced off the body it had struck and did not pierce it, for the gift of the god held it back. Achilles in his turn attacked noble Agenor, but Apollo would not grant him the glory. He snatched Agenor away and hid him in a thick mist, sending him out of the battle unharmed. Then he cleverly drew the son of Peleus away from pursuing the army. He took on the likeness of Agenor and stood in front of Achilles, who ran toward him to chase him. Achilles pursued him over the grain fields of the plain, turning him toward the deep waters of the river Scamander. Apollo ran only a little way ahead and tricked Achilles, making him think the whole time that he was about to overtake him. Meanwhile the rabble of routed Trojans was glad to crowd into the city until it was packed with them. They no longer dared to wait for one another outside the walls, to learn who had escaped and who had fallen in the fight. All whose feet and knees could still carry them poured into the town in a heap.
